title: The Servant of the LORD
lead: "The servant of the LORD" is first a title of honor and of a task: it is given to Moses, Abraham, David, Job and "my servants the prophets" long before Isaiah. In Isaiah 40–55 the LORD speaks of "my servant" and means sometimes plainly Israel, sometimes a figure with a mission to Israel who suffers and is vindicated (42:1–9; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12). Jewish readers have seen Israel, a prophet or the Messiah in him; the New Testament reads the songs of Jesus, whom it calls God's servant (Greek pais, "servant, child"), and also speaks of believers as servants.

sections.b: "My servant" is said of Moses (Numbers 12:7; Joshua 1:2), of Abraham (Genesis 26:24), of David (2 Samuel 7:5; Ezekiel 34:23–24; 37:24), of Job (Job 1:8; 42:7–8) and, in the plural, of "my servants the prophets" (2 Kings 17:13; Jeremiah 7:25). It is a title of honor and of a task, not of rank: the servant is the one the LORD sends and stands behind. When Isaiah 40–55 calls Israel and then an individual "my servant", it is using a word its hearers already knew.
sections.refs: Numbers 12:7; Joshua 1:2; Genesis 26:24; 2 Samuel 7:5; Job 1:8; 2 Kings 17:13; Jeremiah 7:25; Ezekiel 34:23–24

sections.h: The four songs as a whole
sections.b: In 1892 Bernhard Duhm set apart four passages of Isaiah 40–55 as the 'servant songs': 42:1–4 (God presents his chosen servant, who brings justice to the nations gently), 49:1–6 (the servant, called from the womb and named Israel, is made a light to the nations), 50:4–9 (the servant who listens each morning gives his back to the floggers and trusts God to vindicate him) and 52:13–53:12 (the despised servant, crushed for others' guilt, is exalted). Later scholars often extend the first three to 42:1–9, 49:1–13 and 50:4–11, the ranges used in this site's notes. Read in order, they move from calling to mission, from opposition to suffering, and from death to vindication. Outside the songs, 'my servant' in these chapters is plainly Jacob-Israel (41:8–9; 44:1–2, 21; 45:4; 48:20), sometimes blind and deaf (42:18–20). After 53 the book speaks only of 'servants' in the plural (54:17; 65:8–15). Many scholars now doubt that the songs were ever a separate collection (Mettinger) and read them in their context in the book.
sections.refs: Isaiah 42:1–4; Isaiah 49:1–6; Isaiah 50:4–9; Isaiah 52:13–53:12; Isaiah 41:8–9; Isaiah 54:17

sections.h: Who is the servant? Jewish and Christian answers
sections.b: The question is as old as the Ethiopian's in Acts 8:34: 'about himself or about someone else?'. Israel: Jewish teachers known to Origen (Against Celsus 1.55) read 52:13–53:12 of the people scattered among the nations, and Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi and Abravanel made this the main Jewish reading, citing 49:3 ('You are my servant, Israel'). The Messiah: the Targum of Isaiah names him 'my servant the Messiah' (52:13) but moves the suffering onto Israel and the nations; the Talmud calls the Messiah 'the leper of the house of Rabbi' from 53:4 (Sanhedrin 98b). An individual of the past: Moses (Sotah 14a, on 53:12), Jeremiah (Saadia Gaon; Grotius), Zerubbabel or Jehoiachin (Sellin), or the prophet himself (Mowinckel, Whybray). Jesus: the New Testament and the church. Modern scholars also speak of a 'corporate' figure who moves between the people and one who embodies it (H. Wheeler Robinson), or, reading the book as a whole, of the one who fulfills Israel's task when Israel fails (Childs). Christopher North's The Suffering Servant in Deutero-Isaiah traces the whole history.

sections.h: The servant in the New Testament
sections.b: The New Testament applies all four songs to Jesus. Matthew quotes the first in full at Jesus's healings (Matthew 12:18–21, from Isaiah 42:1–4) and hears its first line in the voice at the baptism (Matthew 3:17). Simeon (Luke 2:32) and Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:47) take up 'a light to the nations' from 49:6, and Paul applies 49:8 to 'the day of salvation' (2 Corinthians 6:2). The Passion narratives echo 50:6. The fourth song is quoted most: 53:1 in John 12:38 and Romans 10:16; 53:4 in Matthew 8:17; 53:7–8 in Acts 8:32–33; 53:12 in Luke 22:37, in Jesus's own words; 53:4–9 throughout 1 Peter 2:21–25; and 52:15 in Romans 15:21. Echoes are widely seen in Mark 10:45, Romans 4:25 and Philippians 2:6–11. Whether Jesus himself understood his death through Isaiah 53 is debated (Hooker against Stuhlmacher and Hengel), but by the time of 1 Clement 16 (about AD 96), which quotes the whole song, the Christian reading was established.
sections.refs: Matthew 12:18–21; Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47; Matthew 8:17; Acts 8:32–35; Luke 22:37; 1 Peter 2:21–25; Romans 10:16; Romans 15:21; Mark 10:45

sections.h: Later reuse inside the Bible and just outside it
sections.b: Zechariah 3:8 has the LORD say, "I am about to bring my servant, the Branch." In Daniel the wise who "make many righteous" (matsdiqe harabbim, Daniel 12:3; compare the maskilim of 11:33–35) are widely seen as echoing Isaiah 53:11, where the servant "makes many righteous". The Wisdom of Solomon (a deuterocanonical book, Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches, not for Jews or Protestants) tells in chapters 2–5 of a righteous man whom the wicked torment and God vindicates, and calls him God's child or servant (pais, 2:13). In the New Testament Jesus is God's pais in Acts 3:13, 26 and 4:27, 30, and Philippians 2:7 says he took "a slave's form", beside the quotations listed above.
sections.refs: Zechariah 3:8; Daniel 12:3; Daniel 11:33–35; Acts 3:13; Acts 4:27; Philippians 2:7
